index.html.text:
PRIVATE, LOCAL-FIRST WORKFLOW

Reconcile processor payouts before they disappear into the bank feed.

Upload two CSV exports, match deposits by amount and date, and leave with a short discrepancy list. Built for small businesses using Stripe, Square, PayPal, or a mix without a full accounting suite.

1. Processor payouts

CSV needs a date and amount column. Common names like payout_date and net work automatically.

2. Bank deposits

CSV needs a date and amount column. Credits should be positive amounts.

Processor payouts can settle a few days after the customer payment. Exact amounts match first; a payout split across nearby deposits is also matched.

Don't have both exports handy? — four payouts against five deposits, carrying one of each result this tool can report.

Review queue

0matched
0payouts not found
0deposits not explained
0exceptions with a likely cause

Where a payout and a nearby deposit almost agree, the What to check column names the gap and whether it looks like a processor fee. It is a lead to verify against your statement, not a match.

Common questions

How close do a payout and a deposit have to be to count as a match?

The same amount to the cent, landing within the date tolerance you set (default 3 days, adjustable up to 30). A payout that settles a few days after the customer payment is expected; the tolerance is there for that gap, not to paper over a real discrepancy.

What if one payout was deposited as several smaller amounts?

The tool also checks whether a payout matches the sum of several nearby bank deposits, searching up to the first 18 eligible deposits per payout to keep the browser work bounded. Each deposit can only explain one payout, so a single deposit is never counted toward two different exceptions. See why one payout shows up as two bank deposits for a worked example, including what happens when the split does not add up exactly.

How is this different from Synder, A2X, or another paid sync tool?

Those connect live to your payment processor and your accounting platform and keep posting transactions automatically, every day, on a paid plan. This workbench has no connection: you choose two CSV files you already exported, it matches them once in your browser, and nothing is kept between runs unless you download the review CSV. See this workbench vs. Synder for the full comparison.

What does the "What to check" column mean?

Where an unmatched payout has a nearby deposit that could explain it, the workbench pairs them and states the gap in money and as a percentage. If that gap falls in the roughly 0.1%–6% range typical of card-processor fees, it says so. Where the amount is exactly right but the deposit landed later than your tolerance allows, it says that instead and names the gap in days, so you can decide whether to widen the tolerance and re-run. Either way this is a lead to verify against your processor statement, not a confirmed match.

Why is a payout unmatched when the deposit is the right amount?

Because the deposit landed outside the date tolerance you set. Banks post a few days after the processor releases a payout, and weekends, holidays, and month-end batches stretch that further. The workbench looks a week past your tolerance when it pairs exceptions, so a row like this reads "same amount, 5 days apart — outside the date tolerance you set" rather than leaving the What to check column empty. Raise the tolerance to cover the gap and run it again, and the pair matches outright.

Does it recognize my processor's CSV format automatically?

It looks for common header names — date, payout_date, deposit_date, net, and amount — which cover typical Stripe, Square, and PayPal exports. If your export uses different column names, rename the header row before uploading.

Is this an accounting system or does it move money?

No. It is a local, browser-only review aid that reads two CSV files you choose and produces an exception list. It does not connect to any payment provider, does not move money, and is not a system of record — download the review CSV if you need to keep the result.

Are my payout and bank files uploaded anywhere?

No. Everything runs in your browser; the files never leave your device. The optional usage counter records only that a reconciliation ran, not any amounts, dates, or file contents.

How is this different from a paid sync tool like Synder?

Synder is a paid subscription that connects to your payment processor and your QuickBooks or Xero account, then posts every transaction and keeps syncing on an ongoing basis. This workbench connects to nothing: you upload two CSV exports you already have and get a one-time review queue, with no account to make, cancel, or pay for. See this workbench vs. Synder for which job fits which situation.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, financial, or accounting advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Everything runs in your browser. Files are never uploaded. Anonymous feature counts are local-only, can be disabled below, and contain no financial data.

Reconciling a landlord's CAM bill instead of processor payouts? The CAM reconciliation calculator checks a tenant's common-area-maintenance share, credits, and billed-charge variance — nothing uploaded.

Checking for a double payment to a vendor instead of matching payouts to deposits? The duplicate payment audit flags likely duplicate or double vendor payments in an accounts-payable ledger export — nothing uploaded there either.

Free and open source. If it caught a reconciliation break, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

const KEY = 'payment-reconciliation-usage';
export function count(event) { if (localStorage.getItem('payment-reconciliation-disable') === '1' || navigator.globalPrivacyControl || navigator.doNotTrack === '1') return; const data = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY) || '{}'); data[event] = (data[event] || 0) + 1; localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(data)); }

vs-reconciling-in-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Payment Reconciliation Workbench

This workbench vs. reconciling in a spreadsheet

A VLOOKUP matches one payout to one deposit at one exact amount. It has no answer when the bank split a payout into two deposits, or posted one a few days later than you scanned for.

What a spreadsheet formula gets right

Pasting a payout export and a bank export into two sheets and running a VLOOKUP or MATCH on the amount column is the ordinary way anyone checks payouts against deposits, and for the common case it works: same amount, landed within a day or two, one row finds the other. Sorting both columns and scanning by eye works about as well for a short list.

What both approaches assume is that every payout corresponds to exactly one deposit row at exactly the amount you are looking up. That assumption holds often enough to feel reliable -- until it doesn't.

A real pair, from this tool's own worked example

This is not a hypothetical. It is the four-payout, five-deposit fixture shipped with this workbench's own "Load a worked example" control, reproduced exactly: 

payouts.csv                    deposits.csv
2026-03-02   1420.00           2026-03-03   1420.00
2026-03-05   2310.50           2026-03-06   1200.00
2026-03-09    890.00           2026-03-06   1110.50
2026-03-16   1750.00           2026-03-10    864.35
                                2026-03-30    455.00

=VLOOKUP(2310.50, deposits, 1, FALSE) returns nothing, because no single deposit row equals $2,310.50 -- the bank actually posted that payout as two rows, $1,200.00 and $1,110.50, three days later. The row is not missing from the export; it is simply not shaped like the amount you looked up. Running this workbench against the same pair instead reports it as one matched payout, explicitly naming both deposit rows that together account for it.

The $890.00 payout is a second, quieter failure: the nearest deposit is $864.35, a $25.65 gap (2.88%) that reads as a processor fee once you know to check the percentage. A sorted scan either has to make that judgment by eye or leave the row as an unexplained gap; this tool states it in one line -- "deposit is 25.65 (2.88%) short — consistent with a processor fee deducted from the transfer" -- still a lead to verify against your statement, not an asserted match.

Side by side

Spreadsheet formula or manual scanThis workbench
A VLOOKUP or MATCH on amount finds a payout only if one deposit row equals it exactly.Also checks whether a payout equals the sum of several nearby deposits, searching up to 18 candidates per payout.
Judging whether a small gap "looks like a fee" is a call the person scanning has to make each time.Computes the gap as a percentage and flags it when it falls in the roughly 0.1%–6% range typical of a processor fee.
A blank amount cell inside a SUM or VLOOKUP range is silently treated as zero.Rejects a row with no digits in its date or amount column before reconciling anything.
An unmatched row has to be noticed while scrolling a sorted sheet.Reports every payout and deposit exactly once, as matched, unmatched, or explained -- nothing to scroll past.
Free, and needs only a spreadsheet you already have.Also free, local, and needs only the two CSV exports you already have.

Using both together

A spreadsheet you already trust, tuned to your own processor's column names and checked against a quarter of statements, is a reasonable thing to keep using. What this workbench removes is the two failure modes above on a file you have not already built formulas for: the split deposit a single-row lookup cannot see, and the late or short deposit a date scan can miss or misjudge.

Open the workbench and load the worked example above, or upload your own payout and bank CSVs — no account, no connection, and it keeps working once the page has loaded. Comparing against a paid, connected sync instead of a spreadsheet? See this workbench vs. Synder.

Common questions

Isn't a VLOOKUP or SUMIFS good enough to match payouts to deposits?

It handles the ordinary case -- one payout, one deposit, the same amount -- well. It breaks on the two cases that actually cost time: a payout the bank split across several smaller deposits, which a single-row lookup cannot see at all, and a deposit that landed a few days late, which either needs a fuzzy formula nobody builds for a one-off check or gets missed on a plain exact-amount match. Both are ordinary occurrences, not edge cases -- this workbench's own worked example produces one of each.

How does the split-deposit case actually break a spreadsheet formula?

On this tool's own worked example, a $2,310.50 payout on March 5 lands at the bank as two separate deposits three days later: $1,200.00 and $1,110.50. A VLOOKUP or MATCH on the payout amount finds nothing, because no single deposit row equals $2,310.50 -- the row is genuinely not there. Finding it requires either noticing two deposits near that date happen to add up, or writing a SUMPRODUCT or Power Query step that checks combinations, which is more spreadsheet engineering than most people build for a single reconciliation run. This workbench searches deposit combinations for a matching sum automatically, up to 18 nearby candidates per payout.

What does a scanned date range miss that this tool doesn't?

On the same worked example, an $890.00 payout has no exact deposit match, but a $864.35 deposit landed nearby -- a $25.65 gap, 2.88% of the payout, which is inside the roughly 0.1%-6% range typical of a processor fee. A person scanning a sorted list for 'close enough' either has to remember what a normal fee percentage looks like or skip the judgment entirely and leave the row as a flat unexplained gap. This tool computes the percentage, checks it against that range, and states the reading in one sentence -- still a lead to verify against your statement, never an asserted match.

A blank amount cell in a spreadsheet formula is easy to miss -- what happens here?

In a spreadsheet, a blank cell inside a SUM or VLOOKUP range is silently treated as zero -- the formula still returns a number, so nothing flags that a row was incomplete. This workbench's CSV reader checks every date and amount cell before reconciling anything: a row with no digits in its amount column, or a date it cannot parse, stops the run with an error naming the file, rather than quietly reconciling a phantom $0.00 payout or deposit.

Does this replace building my own reconciliation spreadsheet?

Not for every case -- a spreadsheet you already trust, already customized to your own processor's CSV columns, and already checked against a quarter of statements is a reasonable thing to keep using. What this tool removes is the two failure modes above on a file you have not already built formulas for: the split deposit a lookup cannot see, and the late deposit a date scan can miss or misjudge. It runs entirely in your browser on the two CSVs you already exported, with nothing to connect and no formula to maintain between runs.

vs-synder.html.text:
← Payment Reconciliation Workbench

This workbench vs. Synder

Synder is a paid, ongoing sync tool. You connect a live payment source — Stripe, Square, PayPal, Amazon, and others — and a live accounting destination — QuickBooks Online, Xero, or Sage Intacct — and it posts categorized transactions and matches deposits automatically, running every day, on transaction-volume-based paid plans described on synder.com.

Different jobs, at different points

That makes Synder the right choice for one job: keeping the books current automatically, every day, from accounts it stays connected to. This workbench does not do that job. It has no connection, no daily sync, and no accounting destination — it reads the two CSV files you choose, matches them once, and the review queue is gone when you close the tab unless you download it.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want my QuickBooks or Xero books to stay current automatically as Stripe, Square, or PayPal payouts land, every day, without touching a CSV.Synder — that is a live, connected sync job this workbench does not do.
I have two CSV exports right now — processor payouts and a bank statement — and want to see which payouts have reached the bank, today, without connecting anything.This workbench — choose the two files, set a date tolerance, run it, no account and nothing linked.
I don't use QuickBooks, Xero, or Sage, or I don't want to grant a third party standing access to my payment processor and bank accounting connection just to check one batch.This workbench — it has nothing to connect to and asks for no ongoing access.
One payout landed as several smaller bank deposits and I need to know if they add up.This workbench's grouped matching, or Synder's transaction sync — both handle a split deposit; this workbench explains its rule on its split-deposit worked example.
I want a categorized, auditable transaction history inside my accounting platform, going back months, that updates on its own.Synder — that is an ongoing bookkeeping record this workbench never keeps; it produces one exception list per run and stores nothing between runs.

Some businesses use a tool like this one for a quick check before committing to a paid, connected sync, or for the processors and accounting setups Synder does not cover; others use Synder because the daily automation is the point. The two are not substitutes for each other.

Open the workbench and upload your own payout and bank CSVs — no account, no connection, and it keeps working once the page has loaded.

Common questions

Should I use this workbench or Synder?

They answer different questions at different points in the bookkeeping cycle. Synder is a paid, ongoing sync: you connect a live payment source such as Stripe, Square, PayPal, or Amazon and a live accounting destination such as QuickBooks Online, Xero, or Sage Intacct, and it posts categorized transactions and matches deposits automatically, every day, described on Synder's own site. This workbench has no connection and no ongoing sync. You choose two CSV files you already exported, it matches them once in your browser, and the review queue disappears when you close the tab unless you download it. A business that wants its books kept current automatically, every day, wants Synder. A business that wants to check one batch of payouts against the bank right now, without linking a payment processor or an accounting platform, wants this workbench.

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Synder. Synder is named here only to describe what this workbench is and is not, based on Synder's own public site and integration documentation.

why-does-one-payout-show-up-as-two-bank-.text:
← Payment Reconciliation Workbench

Why does one payout show up as two (or more) bank deposits?

A processor sometimes releases a single payout as more than one bank transfer, or the bank simply posts it in pieces. The table below is the exact fixture the workbench's own test suite uses to confirm a split deposit is matched as one group, not left as two unexplained rows.

One payout, two deposits, three days

A $100.00 payout on 2026-08-20 lands as a $60.00 deposit on 2026-08-21 and a $40.00 deposit on 2026-08-22 — both inside a 3-day tolerance, and $60.00 + $40.00 = $100.00 exactly.
RowDateAmount
Payout2026-08-20$100.00
Deposit 12026-08-21$60.00
Deposit 22026-08-22$40.00

Group total: $60.00 + $40.00 = $100.00, matching the payout to the cent. Both deposits are inside the 3-day date tolerance, so the workbench marks all three rows matched instead of leaving two unexplained deposits and one unexplained payout.

The search is bounded so a large export cannot freeze the browser: it looks at the first 18 eligible deposits near a payout (sorted largest amount first), and only accepts a group of up to 8 of them. A group is accepted only when its total equals the payout exactly — the workbench never guesses that a near-enough sum is close enough, because a genuine discrepancy would then hide inside a false match.

Open the workbench and upload your own payout and deposit CSVs to see this grouping run on your own data. Nothing you upload is sent anywhere.

This page is arithmetic, not accounting or financial advice. It does not tell you whether a discrepancy is acceptable and does not replace review by a qualified professional.

Common questions

Why does one payout show up as two or more bank deposits?

A processor sometimes releases a single payout as more than one bank transfer, or the bank posts it in pieces. A $100.00 payout landing as a $60.00 deposit one day and a $40.00 deposit the next is matched as a single group because the deposits fall inside the date tolerance and sum to the payout exactly. The workbench searches up to the first 18 eligible deposits near a payout, groups up to 8 of them largest-first, and only accepts a group whose total equals the payout to the cent.

What if the split deposits do not add up exactly, for example a fee was taken from one of them?

Group matching only accepts an exact sum, so a fee deducted from one leg of a split deposit breaks the total and the group is not formed. The payout is reported as an exception instead, and the workbench pairs it with the nearest unmatched deposit as a lead: for a $100.00 payout against a $96.80 deposit it reads deposit is 3.20 (3.20%) short — consistent with a processor fee deducted from the transfer. That is a hint to verify against the statement, not a match.

Can the same bank deposit end up explaining two different payouts?

No. Once a deposit is used in a matched group, or offered as the explanation for one exception, the workbench marks it used and will not offer it again. That keeps the review queue from double-counting a single deposit toward two different payouts.
